This page corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 29-2011.04 occupation "Histotechnologists" (histotechnologists): applying knowledge of health and disease causes to evaluate new laboratory techniques and procedures for examining tissue samples; processing tissue sections and preparing histological slides for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists; and possibly solving technical or instrument problems or assisting with research studies. Official scope text: Apply knowledge of health and disease causes to evaluate new laboratory techniques and procedures to examine tissue samples. Process and prepare histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists. May solve technical or instrument problems or assist with research studies. The U.S. wages on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 data presented by O*NET, labeled on the page as the clinical laboratory technologists and technicians (29-2011.00) parent scope; the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; the two jurisdictions and their systems must not be applied to one another.

To judge whether to enter histotechnology, first run one verifiable preparation task using public or simulated materials: choose a clear type of tissue sample (for example, a tissue block from a surgically resected specimen), complete a step-by-step plan from receipt, fixation, dehydration, embedding, sectioning, to staining and coverslipping, spelling out the operating conditions, quality control points, possible abnormalities (wrinkled sections, uneven staining, detached sections, contamination), and how to handle them, and keep a reviewable record template. Afterward, check: whether specimen identification and consistency with patient information are treated as the first step, whether abnormalities and situations beyond your authority are written as stop-and-escalate, and whether each step produces a traceable record. Finally, mark which matters exceed your individual operating and sign-off authority (pathological diagnosis, report issuance, test conclusions) and, following institutional rules, explain to whom they should be escalated. Test with a real deliverable, not just answers to an interest questionnaire.

Fit signals | The work activity importance ratings for U.S. O*NET 29-2011.04 show that documenting/recording information (78), inspecting equipment, structures, or materials (78), communicating with supervisors, peers, or subordinates (75), evaluating information to determine compliance with standards (71), making decisions and solving problems (70), and monitoring processes, materials, or surroundings (69) are the most important activities for this occupation; work context shows that indoors, environmentally controlled 100% report every day, time pressure 90% report every day, manual dexterity 86% report continually or almost continually, wearing common protective or safety equipment 90% report every day, exposure to hazardous conditions 86% report every day, exposure to contaminants 81% report every day, electronic mail 81% report every day, face-to-face discussions 67% report every day, importance of being exact or accurate 57% report extremely important and 38% report very important, and responsibility for others' health and safety 29% report very high responsibility and 33% report high responsibility. The most important skills are reading comprehension (63), judgment and decision making (60), critical thinking (60), and monitoring (60). If you are willing to do fine work to procedure in a controlled environment over the long term, keep every step as a reviewable record, and be able to stop and escalate within the time an abnormality allows, these daily demands are closer to the way you work.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows (29-2011.04): indoors, environmentally controlled 100% report every day, exposure to hazardous conditions 86% report every day, exposure to contaminants 81% report every day, time pressure 90% report every day, manual dexterity 86% report continually or almost continually, physical proximity 62% report moderately close (at arm's length), and working hours 70% report 40 hours and 30% report more than 40 hours. This occupation deals with tissue samples, slides, and patient information; a single specimen identification error or a single section or staining quality failure carries the error into the pathological diagnosis, and a single mishandling of patient information creates privacy and compliance risks. This page therefore lists health risk control, infection control, patient information protection, and practice/supervision boundaries separately, and stresses that abnormalities require stopping and escalating rather than an individual deciding on their own. On the U.S. side, this occupation itself is not marked Bright Outlook, and the O*NET summary shows the broad group it belongs to is projected to grow below average (1%—2%) from 2024 to 2034. If you find it hard to sustain fine repetitive work and time pressure in a controlled environment, or are unwilling to take responsibility for recording every step and for patient safety, you should treat these as real costs that need careful weighing.

Commitment judgment | Real fit comes from whether you can do three things on the same batch of samples at once: make the preparation solid (complete fixation, dehydration, embedding, sectioning, staining, and coverslipping to procedure, producing reviewable slides, quality control records, and batch records); keep quality and safety boundaries under control (consistency between specimens and patient information, infection control and protection, stopping and handling abnormalities and out-of-control samples to procedure, and handling patient information under institutional rules); and carry definable position responsibility (be responsible for the operations you complete and the truthfulness of records, while referring matters beyond operating authority, such as pathological diagnosis, report issuance, and test conclusions, to qualified personnel or bodies under institutional rules). It is recommended to test this with one verifiable experience (completing a step-by-step preparation plan and record template, one drill on recognizing and handling common abnormalities, or a review of one quality control failure), rather than relying only on the conclusions of an interest questionnaire.

The daily work of histotechnologists can be broken down along three lines: (1) specimens and preprocessing—receipt, identification, fixation, dehydration, decalcification, and embedding; (2) sectioning and staining—sectioning, routine and special staining, reagent preparation, and coverslipping; (3) quality and support—quality control and instrument maintenance records, handling abnormalities, and organizing materials for pathological diagnosis and research. The three lines share the same set of operating standards and record requirements, but their deliverables go to different recipients: preprocessing and sectioning feed the downstream reading step, quality control and records serve the laboratory quality system, and research support serves research projects.

Conclusion | Histotechnologists differ from adjacent occupations in sample types, methods, and authorization boundaries: the core of this occupation is turning tissue samples into readable histological slides while ensuring quality; biological technicians and chemical technicians use their own experimental systems and test objects; pathologists (physicians) are responsible for diagnosis; microbiologists focus on microbiological testing; and medical clinical technologists have a broader scope covering many kinds of testing. Swapping them based only on job title would misjudge authorization and responsibility.

entries.answer: According to O*NET 29-2011.04, this occupation applies knowledge of health and disease causes to evaluate laboratory techniques and procedures for examining tissue samples, and prepares histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists. Typical tasks include paraffin embedding (importance 97), sectioning (94), staining (93), organizing materials for pathologists (91), maintaining records (87), and examining slides under a microscope (82).
entries.question: What exactly do histotechnologists do?

entries.answer: Clinical laboratory technologists and technicians cover a broader scope and many kinds of testing; biological technicians and chemical technicians use their own experimental systems and test objects; pathologists (physicians) are responsible for diagnosis and sign reports; microbiologists focus on microbiological testing. These directions differ in authorization and responsibility boundaries and cannot be swapped based only on job title.

subject.summary: Histotechnologists corresponds to the precise U.S. O*NET/SOC 29-2011.04 occupation "Histotechnologists": applying knowledge of health and disease causes to evaluate laboratory techniques and procedures for examining tissue samples, processing tissue sections and preparing histological slides for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists; they may also solve technical or instrument problems or assist with research studies. Official scope text: Apply knowledge of health and disease causes to evaluate new laboratory techniques and procedures to examine tissue samples. Process and prepare histological slides from tissue sections for microscopic examination and diagnosis by pathologists. May solve technical or instrument problems or assist with research studies. Core tasks include paraffin embedding (importance 97), sectioning (94), staining (93), organizing materials for pathologists (91), maintaining records (87), and examining slides under a microscope (82). The U.S. wages and employment on this page come from BLS OEWS 2025 data presented by O*NET, labeled on the page as the clinical laboratory technologists and technicians (broad group) parent scope; the precise occupational wage for mainland China was not obtained and is registered as a visible gap; China's institutional boundaries are labeled separately under the Basic Medical Care and Health Promotion Law and the Personal Information Protection Law.
